rows.label: Long-run gain in GDP per capita from a permanent transition to democracy (share)

source.title: Acemoglu, Naidu, Restrepo and Robinson (2019), Democracy Does Cause Growth, Journal of Political Economy 127(1): 47-100
source.page: p. 59 (text) and p. 60 (table 2, column 3, the preferred specification)
source.quote: the implied long-run impact is a 21.24 percent (standard error = 7.21 percent) increase in GDP per capita
source.note: Range: the 95% interval from the standard error (21.24 ± 1.96 × 7.21). Panel of 175 countries, 1960-2010, with country fixed effects; the propensity-score and doubly robust estimates plateau at about 24% (p. 76). With country-specific trends the long-run effect is 6.1% (p. 70, note 13), inside the range.

rows.explainer: What a country gains in income per person, in the long run, from becoming and staying a democracy rather than staying a non-democracy: about a fifth (7% to 35%). The anchor for valuing a better or worse functioning democracy: work that keeps a democracy from sliding into autocracy averts a loss of this size; a smaller reform within a democracy gets a ranged share of it, said and anchored in its model. Income gains enter as ln(1 + gain × share) per person-year × $uov_per_ln_consumption, after the build-up (democratization_years_to_effect).

rows.label: Years until most of democracy's income gain is realized

source.title: Acemoglu, Naidu, Restrepo and Robinson (2019), Democracy Does Cause Growth, Journal of Political Economy 127(1): 47-100
source.quote: We find that 25–30 years after a transition to democracy, most of the long-run gains from democracy in terms of GDP are realized
source.note: Low: the semiparametric estimates plateau between 20 and 25 years (p. 76).

rows.explainer: Democracy's income gain builds up over about 25 years (20 to 30). A model crediting a change in how well a country is governed counts the gain as it builds, not the full long-run gain from the first year: a change brought forward (or a slide put off) by N years ($win_years_counted) moves the whole build-up by N years, worth (1 - (1+r)^-N) × (1 - (1+r)^-T) / (ln(1+r)² × T) full-gain years at rate r over this T (N undiscounted; about 2.9 at 4%, N = 5, T = 25).

rows.label: Bribes paid each year, as a share of GDP (world)

source.title: IMF Survey, Fighting Corruption Critical for Growth and Macroeconomic Stability (on IMF Staff Discussion Note SDN/16/05, Corruption: Costs and Mitigating Strategies), 11 May 2016
source.quote: A recent estimate put the annual cost of bribery at around $1.5 to $2 trillion (roughly 2 percent of global GDP).
source.note: High: $2 trillion over 2015 world GDP of about $75 trillion. Low: our judgment, for countries with less bribery than the world average. The IMF note adds that the economic and social costs of corruption, through lost revenue and growth, could be larger than the bribes themselves.

rows.explainer: About 2% of the world's income is paid in bribes each year (1.5% to 2.7%). A bribe is mostly a transfer, so it is a measure of how much is at stake, not the loss itself: a model of anti-corruption work values what changes (revenue collected, spending reaching its purpose, investment) with a ranged share of this, anchored and said. Country-specific figures, where published, replace it in that model with the reason.

rows.label: Income lost to corruption in the EU each year (share of GDP)

source.title: European Commission, EU Anti-Corruption Report, COM(2014) 38 final (3 February 2014)
source.quote: Corruption alone is estimated to cost the EU economy EUR 120 billion per year, just a little less than the annual budget of the European Union.
source.note: EUR 120 billion against EU GDP of about EUR 13.5 trillion in 2013 is about 0.9%, and it counts only lost tax revenue, investment and EU funds (European Parliamentary Research Service, The Cost of Non-Europe in the area of Organised Crime and Corruption, Annex II - Corruption, PE 579.319, 2016, https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2016/579319/EPRS_STU(2016)579319_EN.pdf, p. 46): a floor, the low end. The EPRS study's Scenarios 2 and 3 put the GDP loss at 1.1-1.5% and 1.3-1.7% of EU-28 GDP, counting only corruption above the EU or peer-group average, so floors too; its Scenario 1, which the authors take as the benchmark while calling it very optimistic, is 4.9-6.3% (pp. 42-43). Best 1.6%, the top of Scenario 3, above both floors and well short of Scenario 1; high 5%, Scenario 1's lower end.

rows.explainer: What corruption costs the EU's economy each year: about 1.6% of income (0.9% to 5%), above the European Commission's EUR 120 billion and the European Parliament study's floors and short of its benchmark scenario. Already a loss of income, not bribes paid, so a model applies it directly. Read by models of anti-corruption work for the share of the people they govern who live in the EU, in place of the world's bribery_share_gdp.

rows.label: Share of public investment's potential value lost to inefficiency, advanced economies

source.title: IMF Survey, Closing Efficiency Gaps Means Big Gains for Public Investment (on IMF Policy Paper, Making Public Investment More Efficient, June 2015)
source.quote: AEs facing a gap of 13 percent on average.
source.note: 134 countries. The range is our judgment around the IMF's average: the paper gives no interval. The survey adds that strengthening public investment management could close up to two-thirds of the gaps.

rows.explainer: In rich countries about an eighth of what public investment could deliver is lost to poor selection, management and corruption (8% to 20%). With the two rows below, the anchor for valuing better-run government: the money at stake is public spending × the gap, and a reform closes a ranged share of it.

rows.label: Share of public investment's potential value lost to inefficiency, emerging markets

source.title: IMF Survey, Closing Efficiency Gaps Means Big Gains for Public Investment (on IMF Policy Paper, Making Public Investment More Efficient, June 2015)
source.quote: EMs facing a gap of 27 percent.
source.note: The range is our judgment around the IMF's average: the paper gives no interval.

rows.explainer: In emerging markets about a quarter of public investment's potential value is lost (18% to 36%).

rows.label: Share of public investment's potential value lost to inefficiency, low-income developing countries

source.title: IMF Survey, Closing Efficiency Gaps Means Big Gains for Public Investment (on IMF Policy Paper, Making Public Investment More Efficient, June 2015)
source.quote: LIDCs facing a gap of 40 percent.
source.note: The range is our judgment around the IMF's average: the paper gives no interval.

rows.explainer: In low-income developing countries about two fifths of public investment's potential value is lost (30% to 50%).

rows.label: Chance per year that a won electoral or governance reform is repealed or overridden

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on the record of US local voting-method reforms (Wikipedia, Ranked-choice voting in the United States, sections Repeals and Bans on use; Wikipedia, Approval voting)
source.quote: As of March 2026, ranked-choice voting has also been banned in nineteen states.
source.note: Modern local reforms: about 47 US cities used ranked-choice voting in April 2025; repealed after 2 to 7 years were Ann Arbor (1974-1976), Pierce County (2006-2009), Burlington (2005-2010), Aspen (2007-2010) and North Carolina's judicial pilot (2006-2013), and Telluride later: roughly 1-2% a year before the state bans of 2022-2026 (the page's list of banning states names 18). Approval voting: Fargo (adopted 2018) ended by North Dakota's 2025 ban after 7 years; St. Louis (2020) kept it when voters passed Proposition R in 2022 (the Center for Election Science, https://electionscience.org/education/st-louis-success: 'passed with 69% support') and was exempted from Missouri's 2024 Amendment 7 (KCUR, 5 November 2024, https://www.kcur.org/politics-elections-and-government/2024-11-05/missouri-amendment-7-ranked-choice-voting-noncitizen: 'St. Louis will continue to use approval voting because it was implemented before the Amendment 7 ban'): one repeal in about 13 city-years. Early 20th-century proportional representation (single transferable vote): used in about 24 US cities before 1940 (the same page, History), Ohio's five repealed after 10 to 34 years (1915-1960), and Cambridge, Massachusetts still using it: roughly 4% a year. 3% a year, from 1% (a reform entrenched in a constitution or charter) to 8% (a recent reform facing a hostile state legislature).

rows.explainer: Won reforms of how elections or governments work are often undone: by the voters, a city council, or a state that bans them. 3% a year (1% to 8%). A model counts a won reform's years with this hazard beside the discount rate: pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate + @democracy.electoral_reform_repeal_rate, years_of_impact), years_of_impact being the template row that reads $win_years_counted. Repeal and 'would have come anyway' are separate questions: the reform may be undone before the years counted run out. A reform already repealed counts the years it was in force, not this rate. For a reform whose income gain builds up (democratization_years_to_effect), the hazard enters that fact's brought-forward formula instead, as r = $discount_rate + this rate.

rows.label: Share of contested policy issues on which policy changed within about four years

source.title: Baumgartner, Berry, Hojnacki, Kimball and Leech (2009), Lobbying and Policy Change: Who Wins, Who Loses, and Why (University of Chicago Press), publisher's synopsis
source.quote: sixty percent of recent lobbying campaigns failed to change policy despite millions of dollars spent trying
source.note: 98 US federal issues, sampled at random from those lobbyists were working on (the book's design). The synopsis adds that resources explain less than five percent of the difference between successful and unsuccessful efforts. Range: our judgment.

rows.explainer: A reference class for p_success: on a contested issue, policy changed about 40% of the time (30% to 50%) over a few years, whoever lobbied, and the side with more money was hardly likelier to win. A pending campaign's chance starts here and moves with the issue's own record; a win already in takes the charity's share of its cause instead (Convention 2).

rows.label: Chance the United States stops being classed a democracy before 2030

source.title: Manifold Markets, Will the Economist Intelligent Unit stop classifying the United States as a democracy before 2030? (market probability via the public API)
source.quote: This market resolves to YES if the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) classifies the United States as either a "hybrid regime" or an "authoritarian regime" in any of its Democracy Index reports published before January 1, 2030.
source.note: Market probability 10.7% on 2026-11-14 (21 traders; https://api.manifold.markets/v0/slug/will-the-economist-intelligent-unit). A broader Manifold market, 'Will the United States no longer be a Democracy in the next ten years?', resolving on Freedom House rating the US 'not free' at any point between now and 2033 (https://api.manifold.markets/v0/slug/will-the-united-states-no-longer-be), stood at 28.4% (31 traders). Metaculus asks the same EIU question, but its page and API need a login, so its figure isn't used. V-Dem's Democracy Report 2026 moved the US from liberal to electoral democracy and named it one of ten new autocratizers in 2025. Rule: best guess the verified market on the stake itself (the EIU classification before 2030), 11%; low about half of it, 5%, for thin markets that may overstate; high the broader verified market, 28%.

rows.explainer: Forecasters' chance that the United States falls out of the democracies, to a hybrid or authoritarian regime in the Economist Intelligence Unit's index, before 2030: about 11% (5% to 28%). The stake for work against US democratic backsliding: a model credits a share of this chance removed, the loss valued with democratization_gdp_gain.

rows.label: Institutional philanthropy for US democracy work per year (2021-2022)

source.title: Democracy Fund (Griffin, Lobeck, Botero, Cooper, Diggles, McKay and Steffen), Field in Focus: The State of Pro-Democracy Institutional Philanthropy, October 2023
source.quote: By our estimate, institutional philanthropy is currently investing an average of $2.7 to $3.4 billion a year to support democracy.
source.note: 2021-2022, from Candid's grants data and a survey of 70 funders; best guess the middle of the range. Mostly 501(c)(3) funding: the survey data are 501(c)(3) only, Candid's are meant to include 501(c)(4) funding (p. 15), and adding the survey's 501(c)(4) data would raise the total by about 13% (p. 16, note 10). Individual donors are left out (p. 15); 45% of surveyed funders planned to increase giving in 2023-2024 (p. 3). A model scales it to the whole field with its own ranged factor.

rows.explainer: Foundations and other institutions give about $3 billion a year ($2.7 to $3.4 billion, 2021-2022 dollars) to US democracy work: elections, voting rights, the rule of law, civic engagement and the information ecosystem. A model of one organisation's share of the field's resources (Convention 2) divides its spending by this, after the share of the field that does its kind of work and the price change to its year (@cpi).

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain that a slide to a hybrid regime loses

source.title: Acemoglu, Naidu, Restrepo and Robinson (2019), Democracy Does Cause Growth, Journal of Political Economy 127(1): 47-100 (the estimate is for a full democracy-to-autocracy transition), and the Economist Intelligence Unit Democracy Index classes (hybrid regime)
source.note: Acemoglu et al. code a country as democratic or not (democratic while Freedom House rates it Free or Partly Free and Polity is positive); the forecast the US stake rests on (us_democracy_loss_chance_2030) is of a slide to a 'hybrid regime', short of the full autocracy their estimate compares with. Our judgment, anchored on Hungary and Turkey, the nearest cases.

rows.explainer: How much of democracy's income gain (democratization_gdp_gain) a slide to a hybrid regime loses, rather than a full fall to autocracy: 60% (30% to 100%). Hungary and Turkey, the nearest cases, kept elections and markets but lost courts' and the press's independence. Read by every model of work against a US slide.

rows.label: Validity of the cross-country income effect of democracy for the United States

source.title: Acemoglu, Naidu, Restrepo and Robinson (2019), Democracy Does Cause Growth, Journal of Political Economy 127(1): 47-100
source.note: Our judgment: the estimate comes from a panel of 175 countries, most poorer than the US.

rows.explainer: The estimate comes from 175 countries, most of them poorer than the US, where democracy raised growth through investment, schooling and reforms that a rich country already has; a rich country's private institutions may hold up more of its income. Judged 0.8 (0.5 to 1). Read by every model that applies democratization_gdp_gain to the United States.

rows.label: Share of the chance of a US democratic breakdown that a year of the whole pro-democracy field's work removes

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Boese et al. (2021), How democracies prevail: democratic resilience as a two-stage process, Democratization 28(5), and on the catastrophic-risk family's cut per dollar
source.note: Boese et al. abstract: 36 breakdowns in 59 autocratization episodes since 1993, the rest including episodes still under way. The nuclear-security comparison is @catastrophe.nuclear_catastrophe_cut_per_million; Baumgartner et al. (2009) is the source of lobbied_issue_change_rate.

rows.explainer: The whole field's year of litigation, election protection, policy and public education (about $3 billion a year from foundations alone, us_democracy_philanthropy_per_year) against a world without it. No study measures this; judged 4.5% (0.5% to 20%), the geometric middle of a lower anchor of about 1% and the range's high of 20%. From below: once autocratization begins, only one in five democracies manage to avert breakdown (Boese et al. 2021, Democratization 28(5), abstract: 36 breakdowns in 59 episodes since 1993, the rest including episodes still under way), so resistance as a whole (courts, elections, officials, the press, civil society) cuts breakdown by about a fifth; durable judicial constraints and long democratic histories are what let democracies prevail, and the field works largely through the courts and election officials. With organised civil society a fifth to a third of that resistance and a year one of five in the window, a year of the field removes 0.8% to 1.3%; the low end is half that. From above: the catastrophic-risk family's typical cut for nuclear-security work, 0.036% of the risk per $1 million (@catastrophe.nuclear_catastrophe_cut_per_million), would give over 100% at the field's $3-4 billion; 4.5% is about a twentieth of that per dollar, for a field a hundred times larger with steeply falling returns, and the high end of 20% a fifth of it. Resources also explain less than 5% of which side wins on contested US policy issues (Baumgartner et al. 2009, lobbied_issue_change_rate's source). A cut in a chance is counted at its expected value, as the catastrophic-risk family does: the field's work is thousands of cases and campaigns, not one bet, so this isn't a single event.

rows.label: Chance per year that a democratic slide, once it has happened, is undone

source.title: Nord et al. (2025), When autocratization is reversed: episodes of U-Turns since 1900, Democratization
source.quote: 52% of all autocratization episodes become U-Turns, which increases to 73% when focusing on the last 30 years
source.note: Abstract; 90% of U-turns restore democracy. The yearly hazard is our judgment.

rows.explainer: Most recent slides are reversed: '52% of all autocratization episodes become U-Turns, which increases to 73% when focusing on the last 30 years', and 90% of U-turns restore democracy (Nord et al. 2025, abstract). A 5% yearly hazard undoes about 70% of slides within 25 years; judged lower than the 73% because a breakdown to a hybrid regime, the forecast's stake, is harder to undo than an episode stopped earlier (2% to 10%). The loss is treated as ending at reversal, a slight understatement since income recovers at the ramp's pace.

rows.label: The whole US pro-democracy field's money as a multiple of institutional 501(c)(3) philanthropy

source.title: Democracy Fund, Field in Focus: The State of Pro-Democracy Institutional Philanthropy, October 2023
source.note: 501(c)(4) funding would raise the 2021-2022 total by about 13% (p. 16, note 10); individual donors are left out (p. 15); 45% of funders planned to give more in 2023-2024 against 8% less (p. 3). The multiple is our judgment.

rows.explainer: us_democracy_philanthropy_per_year counts only institutional philanthropy to 501(c)(3) work in 2021-2022, but the risk cut is the whole field's. Democracy Fund's own report says 501(c)(4) funding would raise its 2021-2022 total from $6.9 to $7.8 billion (+13%, p. 16, note 10), that individual donors are left out and the field's overall size would be larger (p. 15), and that 45% of funders planned to give more in 2023-2024 against 8% less (p. 3); pro bono legal work is also left out (our judgment). Against that, the report names biases the other way: survey response from growing funders and a broader taxonomy than Candid's (p. 15), and slower individual giving in 2023-2024 (p. 16). Judged 1.5 (1.2 to 2.2): x1.13 for 501(c)(4)s, about x1.15 for real growth to 2024 and x1.15 for individual donors and pro bono, the range covering both directions.

rows.label: Share of US democracy money spent on work acting on a slide directly (litigation, election protection, checks on power)

source.title: Democracy Fund, Field in Focus (2023): the field covers elections and voting, the rule of law and accountability, civic engagement and education, money in politics and the information ecosystem
source.note: The split between direct and other work is our judgment; the report does not give one.

rows.explainer: Democracy Fund's total covers elections and voting, the rule of law and accountability, civic engagement and education, money in politics and the information ecosystem. Litigation, election protection, checks on executive power and election-official support are part of it. Judged 40% (20% to 70%).

rows.label: Effect on a slide of a dollar of the field's other work, against a direct dollar

source.title: charityevals' judgment
source.note: No study measures it; the rest of the field (turnout drives, civic education, local news, money in politics) acts on backsliding less directly.

rows.explainer: The rest of the field (turnout drives, civic education, local news, money in politics) also acts on backsliding, less directly, and so shares in the risk cut. Judged a fifth of a direct dollar's effect (0 to half).

rows.label: Side effect: the good of democracy beyond income, as a share of its income value

source.title: Helliwell and Huang (2008), How's your government? International evidence linking good government and well-being, British Journal of Political Science 38(4)
source.note: Autocratization and Subjective Well-Being: Is There a Macro-Level Effect?, Applied Research in Quality of Life (2026), doi 10.1007/s11482-026-10660-0, abstract. No study gives the size for a slide in a rich democracy; the share is our judgment.

rows.explainer: Living under a democracy is worth more than its income: freedom of speech and assembly, fair treatment by the state, no fear of arrest for opposing the government. Helliwell and Huang (2008) find that the quality of government is linked to life satisfaction beyond its link through income, with the size depending on a country's level of development. Across 165 countries in 2005-2023, autocratization shows no clear overall link with life satisfaction, but a negative one in established democracies on 4 of 8 measures (Applied Research in Quality of Life, 2026, abstract), which supports a value beyond income for a rich democracy and the low end of the range. Judged 30% of the income value (10% to 100%).

rows.label: Side effect: non-fatal state repression and intimidation averted, as a share of the income value

source.title: charityevals' judgment; Protect Democracy's Committee for Safe and Secure Elections (150 trainings with election officials and police in 35 states, its page) is work directly against intimidation
source.note: No study gives a size of non-fatal repression for a US slide; the share is our judgment.

rows.explainer: Autocratizing countries see more state repression: arrests, surveillance, threats against officials, journalists and opponents; work such as Protect Democracy's election-official trainings acts directly against intimidation. Non-fatal harms only, judged 5% of the income value (0 to 20%). Deaths from political violence are left out: US political violence kills tens of people a year, which against 340 million people's incomes and a share of a chance would be under 1% of the result.

rows.label: Side effect: US democracy's effect on democracy abroad, as a share of the US income value

source.title: Boese et al. (2021), How democracies prevail: democratic resilience as a two-stage process, Democratization 28(5)
source.note: They find more democratic neighbours help democracies prevail. The size is our judgment.

rows.explainer: Democracy spreads from neighbours and partners (Boese et al. 2021 find more democratic neighbours help democracies prevail), and a US that left the democracies would weaken that pull worldwide and its support for democrats abroad. Judged 20% of the US income value (0 to 60%).

rows.label: Side effect: backlash and polarization that work for democracy provokes, as a share of the income value

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on state bans on ranked-choice voting after local wins (electoral_reform_repeal_rate's source)
source.note: No study sizes it; our judgment, anchored on state bans on ranked-choice voting after local wins (the repeal rate's source).

rows.explainer: Litigation and campaigns seen as partisan can harden the other side and invite counter-measures (state bans on ranked-choice voting followed local wins, electoral_reform_repeal_rate's source). Judged -5% (-15% to 0).

rows.label: Yearly spending of the US movement for proportional representation, 2016-2025 average (2024 dollars)

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on FairVote's and Protect Democracy Project's Forms 990 and Protect Democracy's 2024 grant to Fix Our House (Schedule I)
source.quote: Fix Our House
source.note: FairVote: $4.1 million a year nominal in 2016-2024 ($4.7 million in 2024 prices; ProPublica's totfuncexpns for 2016-2023 and the 2024 return) × fairvote_pr_share 20%, about $0.9 million. A year of a member's 2024 spending is counted against this average year, so the movement's wins per dollar is what each model credits, and members' 2024 shares can add to more than one.

rows.explainer: The US movement for proportional representation's record: about 103,000 people a year newly electing a council or board by multi-winner ranked ballots over 2016-2025 (85,000 to 115,000), Portland, Oregon (2022) most of it. The movement's yearly win, for a past average of its work.

Net of repeals in the period (the Utah pilots, Burlington's 2010 repeal before its 2021 return).

rows.explainer: Every group working for single-winner ranked-choice voting in the US spent about $19 million a year on average over 2016-2025 ($9 million to $39 million, 2024 dollars), ballot campaigns included: the denominator for one organisation's share of the movement's wins (Convention 2), its own spending included (FairVote's and RepresentUs's among them).

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain a switch to single-winner ranked-choice voting brings

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Drutman and Strano (2021), What We Know About Ranked-Choice Voting, New America (literature review)
source.quote: The most notable benefits of ranked-choice voting so far concern campaign tone and descriptive representation.
source.note: The review finds turnout effects mixed (gains mostly where RCV merges a primary and runoff into one November election) and the effect on polarization and moderate winners unclear for lack of data; John, Smith and Zack (2018, Electoral Studies) find an increase of about nine points in the share of candidates from racial or ethnic minorities in four Bay Area cities. Below proportional representation's share (pr_gain_share, 5%): a single-winner method changes who wins one seat less than a switch to multi-member seats.

rows.explainer: Ranked-choice voting for single seats brings about 2% of the income gain of becoming a democracy (0.3% to 6%): its clearer effects are on campaign tone and who stands and wins, not yet on what governments decide. Judged for a rich democracy, so a reform branch applies no further external-validity step.

rows.label: Share of the people newly under ranked-choice voting, weighted by how much of their city's or county's own elections it covers

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on FairVote, Where is ranked choice voting used? (March 2026)
source.quote: reaching nearly 14 million voters across 22 states and Washington, DC
source.note: Weighted by the people added in 2016-2025 (FairVote's list, 14.45 million): New York City (8.3 million) uses ranked ballots for its city primaries and special elections, decisive in a one-party city, about 0.9 of its own elections; the other cities and counties (about 2.0 million) for all their own offices, 1; Portland, Oregon's mayor and auditor (0.65 million, its council is in the proportional-representation figure) 0.5; Maine (1.4 million) for primaries and federal general elections, 0.5 of a full switch; Alaska (0.7 million) for every state and federal general election, 0.9; Hawaii (1.4 million) only for special federal elections and county vacancies, 0.05. Local part: (8.3 × 0.9 + 2.0 × 1 + 0.65 × 0.5) / 14.45 = 0.68; the models multiply it by local_offices_weight, the share of a full switch a city's own elections bring. Range: ±0.12.

rows.explainer: Most of the people added under ranked-choice voting use it for their city's or county's own elections, New York City's primaries above all: 68% of them, weighted by how much of those elections it covers (55% to 80%). × local_offices_weight, plus rcv_state_federal_coverage, gives the share of a full switch (about 44%).

rows.label: Side effect of a won voting-method reform: fairer elections valued beyond income, as a share of the income value

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Frey and Stutzer (2000), Happiness, Economy and Institutions, Economic Journal 110(466): 918-938
source.quote: Institutional factors in the form of direct democracy (via initiatives and referenda)
source.note: The abstract goes on: '…and federal structure (local autonomy) systematically and sizeably raise self-reported individual well-being'; the authors credit both policies closer to voters' wishes and the value of taking part itself. Below the 30% the Protect Democracy model gives democracy's goods beyond income against a slide (ue_freedom_wellbeing), because a change of voting method within a democracy touches no basic freedoms.

rows.explainer: Voters value having their vote count and a say in who represents them beyond what it does for income: a won voting-method reform (ranked-choice voting, proportional representation) adds about 20% to its income value (5% to 60%). Read by every model of such a reform, as a side effect.

source.quote: As of March 2026, ranked-choice voting has also been banned in nineteen states.
source.note: Most bans came since 2022, many after local or state wins: they repeal existing use (in electoral_reform_repeal_rate) and also close places to future reform, which a past record doesn't show.

rows.explainer: Wins provoke counter-measures: nineteen states have banned ranked-choice voting, closing places to future reform. About −10% of a won voting-method reform's value (−30% to 0). Read by every model of such a reform, as a side effect.

rows.label: Share of a full switch that a reform of a city's or county's own elections brings

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Frey and Stutzer (2000), Happiness, Economy and Institutions, Economic Journal 110(466): 918-938
source.quote: and federal structure (local autonomy) systematically and sizeably raise self-reported individual well-being
source.note: A city's or county's own offices decide its policing, schools in many places, zoning, transit and local services, but not state or federal law: their share of what a resident's governments do for them, against the national democratization gain the reform shares are fractions of. Local autonomy matters to wellbeing in Frey and Stutzer's Swiss cantons. Judged half (30% to 65%).

rows.explainer: A voting reform of a city's or county's own elections changes about half of what a full switch of all of a resident's governments would (30% to 65%): the reform shares (rcv_gain_share, pr_gain_share) are fractions of the national democratization gain. Read by every model of local voting reforms (with rcv_local_coverage and pr_offices_share), and for any rich democracy's local tier (the UK's councils and mayors too): England's more centralised local government sits inside the range.

rows.label: Years of the US redistricting reform movement counted (2008 to 2025)

source.title: Wikipedia, 2008 California Proposition 11
source.quote: California Common Cause was the advocacy group sponsoring the initiative.

rows.explainer: From California's Proposition 11 (November 2008), the first of the wins counted, to 2025 inclusive: the wins are spread over these years and set against the movement's average spending over the same years (a past average).

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain that an independent redistricting commission brings

source.title: McCartan, Kenny, Simko, Ebowe, Zhao and Imai, Redistricting Reforms Reduce Gerrymandering by Constraining Partisan Actors (arXiv 2407.11336)
source.quote: Though commissions generally reduce bias, reforms that restrict partisan actors in multiple ways, like removing veto points (Michigan), are more effective than commissions where parties retain some control (Ohio).

rows.explainer: Taking the maps from legislators to a commission changes how votes become seats, and through that who governs and what is decided: reforms that constrain partisan actors reduce partisan bias and raise competitiveness (McCartan et al., difference-in-differences), and gerrymanders move the median legislator and state policy (Caughey, Tausanovitch and Warshaw 2017, Election Law Journal). But it changes the seat count by a few points in a state, leaves single-member districts and primaries alone, and many maps weren't badly skewed. Judged 1% of democracy's income gain (0.2% to 4%), half the shared figure for single-winner ranked-choice voting (@democracy.rcv_gain_share, 2%) and a fifth of proportional representation's (5%), whose effects on who wins are larger.

rows.label: Yearly spending of the US movement for redistricting commissions, 2008-2025 average (2024 dollars)

source.title: Wikipedia, 2024 Ohio Issue 1 (Citizens Not Politicians redistricting amendment)
source.quote: Citizens Not Politicians reported that it raised $24.8 million for its campaign.

rows.explainer: The money behind commission reforms only, since the wins counted are commissions: ballot campaigns (Ohio's 2024 Citizens Not Politicians alone raised $24.8 million and lost; California's Propositions 11 and 20, Michigan's Voters Not Politicians, Colorado, Utah, Virginia, Ohio 2015 and 2018, Missouri), about nine state campaigns over the 18 years at $3 to $25 million each, so about $6 million a year; and the standing organisations' work for commissions (Common Cause's own redistricting column was $2.5 million in the year to June 2025 and $7.7 million the year before; the League of Women Voters, RepresentUs, state coalitions), $8 to $20 million a year. Fair-maps litigation is left out, because its wins (court-drawn maps in Pennsylvania 2018, North Carolina 2019, Wisconsin 2024) aren't counted here either. Judged $22 million a year ($12 to $45 million): the denominator for one group's share of the wins (Convention 2), Common Cause's and the Education Fund's own spending included.

rows.label: Share of an independent commission's effect that the weaker redistricting reforms deliver

source.title: McCartan, Kenny, Simko, Ebowe, Zhao and Imai, Redistricting Reforms Reduce Gerrymandering by Constraining Partisan Actors (arXiv 2407.11336)
source.quote: reforms that restrict partisan actors in multiple ways, like removing veto points (Michigan), are more effective than commissions where parties retain some control (Ohio).

rows.explainer: Where legislators keep a hand the reform delivers less: Ohio's commission maps were struck down repeatedly and used anyway, Utah's legislature set its commission's maps aside until a 2025 court order, and Virginia's commission deadlocked (its supreme court's special masters then drew fair maps). Judged 30% (10% to 60%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment for a redistricting commission's effect on how states are governed

source.title: Caughey, Tausanovitch and Warshaw (2017), Partisan Gerrymandering and the Political Process: Effects on Roll-Call Voting and State Policies, Election Law Journal 16(4): 453-469 (MIT open-access copy)
source.quote: partisan gerrymandering has major consequences not only for who wins elections but for the political process as a whole.

rows.explainer: Confidence that commission maps change how states are governed, beyond the gain share's own range: the effect of maps on legislators and policy comes from panel studies of efficiency gaps (Caughey et al. 2017), the commissions' effect on bias from one difference-in-differences study, and the income effect from cross-country democracy. Judged 0.6 (0.3 to 0.9), the shared figure for proportional representation (@democracy.pr_evidence_adj, 0.6) and above ranked-choice voting's (0.5): the link from maps to policy is better studied.

rows.label: A dollar of other reform work (voting access, money in politics, ethics, media) against a dollar of the redistricting movement

source.title: Thompson, Wu, Yoder and Hall (2020), Universal vote-by-mail has no impact on partisan turnout or vote share, PNAS 117(25): 14052-14056 (authors' copy)
source.quote: We find that universal vote-by-mail does not appear to affect either party's share of turnout

rows.explainer: Voting-access reforms (automatic and same-day registration, mail and early voting), money-in-politics rules (disclosure, small-donor matching), ethics and media policy count through any change in who is elected or what is decided, not per vote (the family's rule). The evidence for that change is thinner than for maps: universal mail voting raised turnout about 2 points and changed neither party's share (Thompson, Wu, Yoder and Hall 2020, PNAS), while maps move the median legislator and state policy (Caughey et al. 2017). Judged a quarter of what a dollar of the redistricting movement does (5% to 100%), the redistricting branch's chain being the nearest one measured for reforms within a US democracy.
